title.en: Irrigation and multipurpose river valley projects

text.en: Rain in India is seasonal and irregular, so farmers need artificial watering. Wells, tanks and canals have fed fields for centuries.

Irrigation is watering plants by artificial means, needed because rain is seasonal and irregular.
Sources: wells (tube wells about 46 percent, other wells 16 percent), canals (24 percent), tanks (3 percent) and others (11 percent).
Canal irrigation suits low relief, fertile soil and perennial rivers; about 60 percent of canal area lies in the northern plains.
Tube wells are common in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Punjab, Madhya Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
Tank irrigation is popular in peninsular India because of undulating relief, hard rocks, few perennial rivers and natural depressions.
Modern methods: drip irrigation (saves up to 70 percent water), sprinkler, rain gun and central pivot.
Multipurpose river valley projects serve irrigation, hydropower, flood control, drinking water, fisheries and navigation.
Examples: Bhakra-Nangal on the Sutlej, Hirakud on the Mahanadi, Damodar Valley, Tungabhadra, Nagarjuna Sagar, Sardar Sarovar on the Narmada and Mettur on the Cauvery.
Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana aims at more production using water saving technologies.

problem.en: Why is tank irrigation popular in peninsular India while canal irrigation is popular in the northern plains?

text.en: The peninsula has hard rock and undulating relief, so canals and wells are difficult to dig.
It lacks perennial rivers but has natural depressions to hold water.
The northern plains have flat land, deep soil and perennial rivers.
